title: Can radial arms give exactly three angles of symmetry?
description: Three equal radial arms are placed round a dot, and the full turn is shared between their three gaps. The turns that fit are counted, with the full turn included. Keeko's doubt is that three angles of symmetry needs four arms, because the full turn is not counted.
teaching_notes: One idea: equal arms at equal gaps give as many angles of symmetry as there are arms, and the full turn is one of them. Watch for students who leave the full turn out of the count.

source: Can we get a figure having exactly 3 angles of symmetry? Can
video_script.why: The child builds a figure with exactly three angles of symmetry from three equal radial arms.
video_script.substitution: three equal radial arms round a dot, with the gaps between them found from the full turn
video_script.anchor: three equal radial arms round a dot, drawn the way the book draws radial arms
video_script.wrong_answer: three angles of symmetry needs four arms
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko does not count the full turn, so Keeko asks for one arm more.
video_script.payoff_line: Three equal arms placed one hundred twenty degrees apart give three angles

final_answer.value: Yes: use 3 equal radial arms placed 120° apart
final_answer.spoken: yes, use three equal radial arms placed one hundred twenty degrees apart

hold_back: Yes: use 3 equal radial arms placed 120° apart
maths_rules: 3 angles of symmetry means 3 turns that fit, and the full turn 360° is one of them
3 equal arms with equal gaps: each arm lands on the next arm
the 3 gaps share the full turn: 360 ÷ 3 = 120
n equal arms at equal gaps give n angles of symmetry
video_script.design: Three equal arms round a dot, with a counter that fills at each turn that fits. Keeko's doubt is that the full turn is not counted.
